Only democracy seems to offer this hope to mankind at large, * the opportunity to regain their Christian concept of human dignity and worth.
The thing that challenges us here and challenges men in all governments and in all parliaments of the world is how to proceed to bring about better conditions which will offer greater hope to the peoples of this world. I would suggest that the answer is to be found in Mr. Churchill's speech on March 5 at Fulton. But first let me go back in years and call attention to the history of the British navy, a navy which helped to keep peace in the world during the century prior to 1914. It was its dominance of the sea lanes and the fact that both Britain and America sought trade, and not war. They were keeping the sea lanes open for commerce. Had Great Britain or the United States been aggressive, warlike nations, their two navies during the past century undoubtedly would have clashed, but they were both dominated by the same thought, that by keeping the sea lanes open for commerce they would produce a better livelihood for all and would raise the standard of living of all the peoples of the world. We can bring the same idea down to our own communities by showing the necessity for law enforcement. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that but for law enforcement we would to-day be harricading our homes or building walls around our industry. We might be unable to trade at all. Mr. Churchill showed a solution when he said:
I have, however, a definite and practical proposal to make for action. Courts and magistrates cannot function without sheriffs and constables. The united nations organization must immediately begin to be equipped with an international armed force. In such a matter we can only go step by step; but we must begin now. I propose that each of the powers and states should be invited to dedicate a certain number of air squadrons to the service of the world organization. These squadrons would be trained and prepared in their own countries but would move around in rotation from one country to another. They would wear the uniform of their own countries with different badges. They would not be required to act against their own nation but in other respects they would be directed by the world organization. This might be started on a modest scale and grow as confidence grew. I wished to see this done after the first world war and trust it may be done forthwith.
As an airman I have flown over a good part of this world and I have a realization of how small it is. Mr. Willkie has given us a lead as to the size of the world to-day when he said:
Continents and oceans are plainly only parts of a whole, seen, as I have seen them, from the air. England and America are parts. Russia and China. Egypt, Syria and Turkey, Iraq and Iran are also parts. And it is inescapable that 
there can be no peace for any part of the world unless the foundations of peace are made secure throughout all parts of the world.
With all the force that I have I endorse the suggestion that Mr. Churchill made that we should start law enforcement throughout the world to-day, on a small scale, not so large that any country could say it was an aggressive force. But let us have the beginning, the nucleus, just as the British navy had its beginning in policing the world and played such a part in keeping the peace and expanding the trade of all nations.
I conclude by quoting again from Mr. Churchill:
Our supreme task and duty is to guard the homes of the common people from the horrors of another war.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks are going to be short this evening. Last session in my first speech I made the remark that coming here'as a newcomer and an industrial worker this institution had for me an air of unreality, and that it was operating in a vacuum. I did not know at the time whether I had made a mistake or not in so describing it, but the more I have seen of it the more I realize that my first impression was right. We dealt on an international plane with such things as atomic energy-a beautiful phrase-it was to be used for the benefit of all mankind, but since that date we have had to arrest some of our leading scientists who have been dealing with atomic energy.
In the United States a great many scientists are quitting in disgust because all the research is going into the' bomb, not into peace-time uses for atomic energy. More and more the state is interfering with and hindering the development of science. We are rapidly moving into the conditions of which we accused the nazis. At one time Great Britain. and Canada were so sure of themselves that they could allow all the world to come in and witness what they are doing. We knew that our modem technology could keep us far ahead of the other fellow. But now there is a different set of conditions; we are frightened of the things we are creating. One thing I notice-and we can disregard the political set-up for the moment-atomic energy developed in Russia will not upset any capital structure, but atomic energy developed in this country is apt to upset too many people's apple-carts, and they want to keep it down. I am not so much interested in the political set-up or the words of men; I am interested in the development of science and what occurs in human society as that development con-

The Address-Mr. Archibald
tinues. In the United States scientists are afraid that we are heading toward a military dictatorship.
We also joined in the Bretton Woods agreement. Since that time Russia has had to go her own way and has been making bilateral agreements with all the border states. It is what is called the barter system of trading; bookkeeping is all that takes place; the great god gold does not interfere; there is no necessity of three per cent interest, for everything is settled with goods. Great Britain also signed the Bretton Woods agreement; but since then, through sheer necessity, she has been forced to enter into the same trading arrangements as Russia did, namely, to set up bilateral trade agreements throughout Europe on the bloc basis. Lord Keynes said when he was in New York that if Britain did not get the loan they would have to adopt the bloc system. In spite of the Bretton Woods agreement they still have to use it. It is a method which will yet be developed more widely on the international scale; we are not going -to be tied to this great thing called gold. Mutual Aid is a system which worked perfectly well during the war in the form of lend-lease, and we shall have to return to it and do away with interest rates. I say, therefore, that in spite of the acts of men, in spite of our attempts to put humpty-dumpty back on the wall, the development of natural laws forces, men in certain directions whether they like it or not.
When we were previously assembled in this house we dealt with certain internal problems of Canada. For example, we discussed veterans houses. We spent days arguing about it. The government hedged this way and that; "oh, it was a difficult problem; we were short of lumber; we were short of soil pipe", and everything else. The mayor of Vancouver went back and forth across the dominion; the dominion government sent wires back and forth about using the hotel Vancouver; it was owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway company, and these men, they thought, wanted to destroy it. There was that great god, private property. Then all of a sudden the ex-servicemen marched into the building and occupied it, and we had to recognize the act. After spending days here wasting our time, these men solved the question in a few minutes.
We also spent days in arguing the discharge system, how we should1 allot discharge points to the men overseas, and so on. The air force went on a sit-down strike, and according to Maclean's magazine it was this act which made the government come out with the discharge policy-not any act which was performed here, but the simple act of the
men sitting down. It gives me great pride that I belonged to the air force and that I was a Joe.
Was my hon. friend overseas in the air force?

I was in this country, and do not start casting aspersions because ' I stayed in this country.
In human society forces adjust themselves. If governing bodies do not administer laws in the interest of mankind, social forces adjust themselves just as forces do in nature. When a volcano has to blow, it blows, to relieve the pressure and adjust the equilibrium. That is what happens in human society. I have heard it stated on numberless occasions in this house that we must have laws, that we should respect them, and all that sort of thing, and lawyers here spend hours of time in expressing that point of view. Yet when a government cannot be respected because it is not administering the laws in the interest of the people, the only method open to the workers of this country is direct action. That is what it comes to, without plotting or planning just spontaneously; so do not start looking for red* herrings under bushes.
I should like to deal for a moment with this spy scare. It is a very opportune thing for the government that it came at this time, because of the weakness of the speech from the throne; the resultant publicity has hidden the real issue, which is the speech itself. I look on this spy scare with a rather jaundiced look, I will frankly admit. The labour movement has had so many things happen to it; for instance, the Zinoviev letter in Britain, shortly after the first war, which put the Conservatives in power and threw labour out because they were supposed to be hooked up with a red bogey. In this country, in 1940, in Saskatchewan a man by the name of Mr. Schneider was in a concentration camp because he had sympathies with the nazis. Of course, when the federal elections came on and he was needed in the election he was released during the election to help the Liberal party, and then he went back into the concentration camp again. We also had communists running around this country sabotaging the war effort: some were thrown into gaol and some hid themselves. However, when it became politically opportune for them to come out and split the labour vote, out they came under a new name, the L.P.P., and they were legal then. Just change your name and you are legal. They served their purpose. I would say to the government, I only hope that when you release the members of this political party once again, if they do go to gaol, you do it with a little more finesse
The Address-Mr. Archibald

next time. This is the kind of thing that goes on in the name of law and order; how can one respect them or reconcile such acts with the ethics by which we are supposed to be guided1? I listen to fine phrases expressed in this house, but I know that when an election comes' on I have to have a hatchet up my back, or I am going to "get it." The duality of the thing is what gets me; you use fine phrases here, but when an election comes you will use any weapon you can lay your hands on.
I should like to speak for a moment on the economic problems facing this country. I come from a frontier area, Skeena. Twenty-five or fifty years ago a Liberal regime would have had railroads going in there; townsites would have been laid out, land booms going on, and developments of all kinds. I should like to know what has happened to the Liberals. They have grown old. Where are the Jim Hills and the Sir Henry Thorntons? They are not with us any more. The Prime Minister. (Mr. Mackenzie King) came to Prince Rupert years ago and he could see hotels and drydocks and shops and everything else. Well, there is a big wheat elevator there; it was built before an election, and it is empty. There is a great big drydock there, run by the Canadian National Railways, and it is empty. I have been trying since last September to get a statement from the government on that situation. Good workers have been fired, scattered all over the country, forced into the cities where unemployment is acute. Also in Prince Rupert we have plenty of houses and skilled workers but no policy. The drydock is there; the men are there and the tools are there to do the job. Had the work been done, it would have relieved the housing shortage to the south and at the same time it would have built up something for the country. The poor C.N.R1 I sometimes think it is like the Missouri mule, without pride of ancestry or hope of posterity.
When you approach the government they tell you to go to the C.N.R., and when you go to the C.N.R. they tell you to go to the government. I know what is behind it. That institution exists simply as a butt for the C.P.R., so that we can spend our time criticizing the C.N.R. I post a letter in Jasper to Vancouver. The letter is taken off in Kamloops, held up a couple of hours and put on the C.P.R. That is what you call efficiency under the economy of our railway system. The same thing applies to the whole north country.
We have a railway problem across the north from Winnipeg right into the Peace River. When I was young and in my prime I went 
and filed on a homestead in Fort St. John. Thank goodness, I had enough sense to come out or I would still have been up there and I would have been in very poor shape. Those poor people went there and lived in sod huts in the middle of a side hill or in log shanties, through the cracks of which they could look at the scenery in all directions. They put up with that condition, half frozen, believing, as had been promised, that a railway would be built to the coast. They spent a lifetime hacking out brush and there are now hundreds of homesteads completely deserted. The life work of men and women, as well as human lives, has been sacrificed, just because of an empty political promise. That is all it meant to governments, but human lives were at stake. Some day the government will have to measure i up to its responsibility.	.
From Prince George to Prince Rupert we have what is known as the Skeena highway. Election after election you would see men with a few picks and axes up there chopping another ten yards and then they would drop it. All of a sudden Japan entered the war and started coming down the Aleutian chain, and then the government put in steam shovels, pouring in the material, with the result that the highway went through. Thank goodness, the wkr lasted long enough to serve that purpose. Since that time the road has been completely plugged with snow so that nobody can use it. Between Havelton and Terrace there ' is a stretch of twenty miles forming a C.N.R. right of way. What happens? The dominion government picks up the whole problem in connection with the highway and hands it over to the province, saying, "There it is". Well, people cannot use that stretch because it is a C.N.R. right of way. You cannot drive trucks over it. The result is that the provincial authorities throw it back to the federal government while we are sitting in the middle looking at it.
It is absolutely useless under the present set-up. This work was done as a result of the necessities of war, and it could be used, because the people need it and would like to enjoy the benefits of it. But they cannot. It is a pity there are not more of us up there. Then we could drive trucks through, and the government would see something^ such as happened in connection with the ex-servicemen in Vancouver. Unfortunately, there are not enough of us and I have to make an appeal here.
To-day transportation is the whole keynote of development in the west. You talk about food going to Europe. There are millions of acres there which could be settled; but two or three years from now we might have a glut on the market and prices would fall, and my

The Address-Mr. Gagnon
hon. friends do not like that. Again, if we went into that development it might result in too much money being put into circulation and the banks would not like it. It is a tragic situation, and it seems that the human element is of no consequence.
There is something else to be considered. The government is spending more on larger navies, armies and so on, in a day of atomic warfare, buzz bombs and all the rest of' it, but not enough attention is being paid to the economic side of it. We all know that we won this war because of our productive effort; we won the war because we smashed the productive effort of the enemy. Without decentralizing industry, in a period such as this-if the government believes in preparedness, as seemingly it does-we are building up a larger army, navy and air force, which is like hanging a voodoo sign outside a shack, and expecting that robbers will not enter, because buzz bombs can smash us overnight. And where would the armies be without supplies? This is national suicide. It is criminal negligence.
Not only for social use but to develop the natural resources of the north, we should run a highway from Atlin down behind the panhandle of Alaska to cover the ground-hog coal fields, where there is as good coal as can be obtained in Pennsylvania; also plenty of hydro-electric power. We want to see these things done, and I would urge the government to make the necessary effort so that we may have real freedom and social justice in this country.

The matter which now transcends all others, although it has but a relative importance and should not make parliament forget the numerous problems for which we are in duty bound to find a solution and with which it behooves us to deal at once, is the espionage matter.	*
The right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) on whom lies responsibility for the inquiry in that matter, deserves high commendation for the course of action he has taken. I find it difficult to understand that anyone should oppose the procedure followed in that matter, which involves a clash between
spies, traitors and communists on the one hand, and the authorities on the other hand, and that such an outcry should be raised against the action of the department of Justice. I should like to speak on behalf of the constituency of Essex West, which comprises chiefly the city of Windsor. I also wish to associate myself with the mover (Mr. Viau) and the seconder (Mr. Winters) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to express my appreciation of being associated with these two hon. gentlemen in the same political party. .
In recent months Windsor has gone through rather dark and troubled days. We have seen dark waters. However, I am happy to say that the darkest cloud preceding the dawn has disappeared and we are again seeing daylight. Windsor's contribution to the winning of the

The Address-Mr. Brown
war is known throughout Canada. Our production of the sinews of war, tanks, trucks, automobiles, chemicals, guns and other things used in warfare is well known and contributed largely, I believe, to the overthrow of Germany. In addition, however, we have fought and won a labour war in Canada; and that war having been won, it is my opinion that now the city of Windsor is destined to become one of the. leading industrial centres of the British empire.
At this point I should like to pay my humble tribute to the work of the Minister of Labour (Air. Mitchell) who has stood so loyally, so faithfully and, shall I say, so serenely behind and on top of the principles he has advocated for so many years. On behalf of the city of Windsor I wish to express to him the appreciation we feel for his efforts in our dark and troublesome days. I should ' like also to pay my respects to Mr. Justice Rand who, through his scholarly and learned decision in the Ford Motor dispute, has won the acclaim of people all over Canada, because, after all, that labour battle has set the pattern for all in Canada, and I think all in Canada will show their gratitude to him.
I think we have made our start toward becoming one of the greatest industrial centres of the British empire. During the last session many statements were made in this house in connection with our labour dispute; in fact on one occasion we had a motion to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing the situa-[DOT] tion in my city. But let me say that industry has shown its faith in the city of Windsor.. To-day the Ford Motor Company is building a $600,000 addition to its plant, and many other industries are constructing additions to their premises. For instance, the Packard Motor Car Company recently purchased property in Windsor on which it intends to erect a plant, and many smaller industries are coming into the city, some of which we hope will grow into large plants. In addition, the larger retail outlets of the Dominion of Canada and the United States of America have found it advantageous to purchase properties there, having in mind the erection of large retail establishments.
As I have said already, Windsor is the centre of the automobile industry of the British empire. In addition, we have some 260 industries, with scores of feeder plants supplying parts to the automobile industry. These plants employ many hundreds of men and played a great part in the winning of the war, especially as against Germany. It can also be said that we are the salt of the earth, because we are the largest producers of salt in Canada. In all probability the table salt
used in British Columbia and the rock salt used in Alberta and Manitoba in connection with dairying come from my city. The chlorine for purification purposes also comes from Windsor. Caustic soda, a product of the salt industry, is used for cleansing purposes. We are the centre of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada; we have the larger pharmaceutical plants, such as Parke Davis, Sterling Products, Frederick Stearns, John Wyeth, Jamieson, and so on. Our geographical location is such that we are bounded on the north by lake St. Clair, in front by the Detroit river and on the south by lake Erie. Strange as it may seem, we are south of the pity of Detroit. Essex county, comprising the constituencies of Essex East, Essex South and my own constituency of Essex West, is known as the sun parlour of Canada. We are served by water, by the busiest waterway in the world. We are served by air by both American and Canadian air lines. We have five railroads. We are also served by a tunnel from Detroit, and a bridge; and in addition we have a railroad tunnel, car ferries and so on. We have fine schools, fine churches, and we are rich in historic lore.
All these things, however, are not the reason for the greatness of this district. Our city is not made famous by its great industries, its geographical location or its fine buildings, but by the spirit of its residents in the hearts and minds' of our people. I think it would best summarize the type of people we have if I were to read a reprint from the Labour Gazette of January, 1944, containing the decision of Mr. Justice Rand as arbitrator in the issue between the union and the Ford Motor Company. At page 4 of the reprint Mr. Justice Rand said:
I have had an opportunity of sizing up the leadership of (this union so far as it is* represented by the committee of negotiation. The members are all of English-speaking origin and British citizenship. They have impressed me as being men of the stuff of which ordinary Canadians are made. With the exception of . . .
Then he mentions two individuals.
. . . who are on leave of absence from General Motors at Oshawa as international representatives of the union, they are men with seniority in the Ford plant ranging from ten to eighteen years. They conducted themselves in negotiation with intelligence and reasonableness. I have no doubt their dominating interest is the job of those they represent in that industry, and that their object is to attain for those employees and their families a secure and self-respecting living,_ which seems to be the object of most Canadians. That aim is legitimate, whether or not attainment is possible.
As I have said, that summarizes the opinion of one who has rendered his decision in an impartial and disinterested way.

Like other Canadian municipalities, we have our choral societies, our theatre guilds, our art associations and our handicrafts guilds. We are no different from the rest of the Dominion of Canada.
Situated as we are, the tourist industry is of vital importance. Across the river in the states of Ohio, Michigan, Indiana and Illinois there is a total population, as of the 1941 census, of 23,488,755 persons, and there has been a considerable increase since that time. Figures furnished to me by the department show that the number of tourists from the United States entering Canada in 1938 through all ports was 17,084,525, of whom 3,497,814 entered through the port of Windsor. I do not intend to refer to the figures for the years 1939 through 1944, but the figures for 1945 Show that 17,207,731 tourists entered through all ports and that 5,437,745, or almost one-third, entered through the port of Windsor.
We have many things to show those tourists who want to make short inroads into Canada, who want to stay for only a short period and travel only a short distance. Besides our fine buildings, there are many other things of interest. We have the Baby residence, the oldest building in the city, a building with a great historical background. Nothing has been done about this building by the dominion government, and I would urge the government to take whatever steps are' necessary, in conjunction with the Essex county Historical Association, to see that some funds are appropriated for the restoration of this building as a point of interest for tourists.
In the adjoining constituency of Essex South at Amherstburg there is the Fort Malden museum. This point is just eighteen miles from Windsor, and this locality has tangible memories of such men as Tecumseh, Sir Isaac Brock and Colonel James Baby. I am glad to say that this building has ben restored and improved and is being used quite extensively. Many tourists visit it each year.
There is also the Point Pelee national park, situated on the most southerly point of the mainland of the Dominion of Canada. I do not propose to go into the details of this park at this time, but I should like to mention that through it pass literally thousands of birds migrating to the south. Strange to say, bees also migrate through here to southern climates as well as literally millions of butterflies. This subject would take considerable time to discuss, but suffice it to say that this park is unique in many other ways. The flora found there are found in no other part of Canada, and the same can be said of the wild life.

I should also like to refer to the Jack Miner bird sanctuary which attracts tourists from the United States, Mexico and many parts of Europe. In 1906 Jack Miner started to band wild geese. He did not put a number on the bands of tin or metal which he placed on the birds he caught; he put on a verse of scripture. The birds were then freed and in the course of years they were found all over the eastern parts of -the United States and Canada, as far north as Baffinland, Hudson bay and other northern posts and as far south as South America. Those scriptural verses which were found in all parts of this continent aroused considerable interest. Preachers in northern outposts preached sermons on the verses which had come to them out of the air. The natives of South America have been helped and have learned about the Dominion of Canada and the Jack Miner sanctuary through birds which have come to them out of the air. So it is my hope that as this bird sanctuary has brought literally thousands of tourists who have spent millions of dollars in the Dominion of Canada, nothing will be done either by this government or by any succeeding government to impede the work of this late and great man but rather that the work will continue with the support of the government of the day.
I said a moment ago that we in Windsor have an art association and a handicrafts association. These associations are of vital interest to our tourist business, and they are very practical. The practical nature of the-art association can perhaps best be illustrated by the following incident, showing the effect which it has had on persons outside the Dominion of Canada who are desirous of seeing what Canada has to offer because of what they have seen done by the art association., also by the National Art Association and the National Gallery of Canada.
A short time ago a gentleman came to this city from India. He was asked what places he would like to see and his first request was to see the National Gallery. He was asked why he wanted to see it, and he said that he had just flown here from India and that at each stop he had found an interesting and beautiful painting of a Canadian scene, and at the bottom of each picture was the source, the National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa. So he wanted to see the national gallery. Probably if he did see it he was disappointed. I mention this because the National Gallery of Canada is of practical value to us in my constituency. It encourages the artists who will depict scenes in my own and neighbouring constituencies which will arouse interest outside the Dominion of Canada and make tourists want to see those scenes. Naturally they

I should like to say a word about the National Gallery of Canada, an institution with which I have only recently become acquainted. I went there the other day and here are some of the things I found. The national, gallery is housed in one end of the museum building, five floors of it, if you include the basement. The space was never designed for a national gallery and is hopelessly inadequate. Most of the partitions are made of wood and beaverboard, carefully disguised with painted burlap, all that the government of the day thought it could afford after the first great war. It is not fireproof; it has not even the elementary conveniences of a public building. The storage and shipping space is even worse.
I am interested in the national gallery,' not because it is in Ottawa, but because I believe this work should be centred in one building under one head from which it can disseminate its work to the benefit of my constituency, and that of course applies to every constituency in the dominion.
The staff consists of the director and a crew of fifteen, all told. Yet that small group is responsible not only for the management of the national gallery in Ottawa but for the loan and educational system that covers the dominion from coast to cost. Approximately 150,000 people visit the national gallery every year, and that is a high figure for a gallery in a city of less than 200,000 population. But the really important feature of the gallerys work is that probably over a million citizens outside Ottawa have seen national gallery travelling exhibitions and received the benefit of its other extension services during the year.
I found that the national gallery had undertaken at least four major jobs during the war and successfully accomplished all of them.
First, it maintained its programme in Ottawa throughout the conflict and extended it as a morale builder, as did the national gallery in London and other public galleries nearer the firing line.
Second, it greatly increased its quota of loan exhibitions so that other Canadian cities should benefit during the stress of war.
Third, it planned and put into operation a unique project whereby the Canadian armed forces were generously supplied with pictures for the decoration of recreation rooms, messes and rest huts. These are the pictures that were seen by the gentlemen who flew here from India. More than 30,000 prints were distributed at no cost to the taxpayer, and the British forces were eventually included in the
scheme, which has made Canadian art known almost around the world. The same pictures were later made available to hospitals and also to schools and other educational institutions. I need not mention that even a great many hon. members of this house have availed themselves of the opportunity of obtaining a few of the silk screens and pictures from the national gallery for decorating their offices.
Fourth, at the request of the defence council the director of the national gallery undertook to chair a committee charged with the duty of selecting and directing Canadian artists in depicting Canada's part in the war. Under this plan a number of the foremost artists were commissioned and sent to the various fronts. Their works are now arriving and will be seen in. exhibitions in increasing numbers as the work develops.
Other services included the assembling and forwarding of exhibitions of Canadian arts to the United States, South America and other countries, and the arranging of return exhibitions for Canada. A system of broadcasts to schools has been established telling the story of Canadian art to young people, using small colour reproductions issued and distributed by the gallery at a nominal price.
Looking at the gallery premises and the small staff of workers, I do not know how it is accomplished. What could be done for this country if we had a gallery building worthy of Canada and^ a staff of, say one-tenth the size of the staff of the film board, a staff to include field workers and lecturers, as well as administrative officials. I understand the grant to the national gallery for all purposes has been about $45,000 a year throughout the war, having been reduced from a prewar figure of $135,000. This is no way to treat an institution with such vast potentialities for vital constructive work for Canada at home and abroad.
I am not specially interested in the national gallery as an ornament to the city of Ottawa, but I am interested in the national gallery as a centre from which the benefits of art can rgdiate to every part of Canada, including Essex county in Ontario. A new national gallery building with adequate storage space, shipping rooms, workshops and galleries is necessary if those of us who cannot come to Ottawa are to share in the great benefits a gallery can produce. Art centres are springing up all over this country, partly as a result of the extension wTork already done by the national gallery but also because of the steadily advancing educational level of the people as a whole. These centres need to be wisely fostered, and only an up-to-date national gallery and a staff with vision can do the job.

Where to-day is the social conscience of the Liberal party? The Progressive Conservatives believe that such conditions should not be tolerated, that no stone should be left unturned to force this government to take adequate action to remedy this housing crisis. I was not active in public life during the worst days of the depression, but when I learned of the conditions that existed I wondered that the people ever stood for them, and I wonder to-day why the people of Canada, in such large numbers, stand for the housing conditions that now prevail. I am quite sure that if they had any kind of leadership many of them would not stand for conditions like that when on every hand they see people who are not only comfortably well off and well housed, but able to acquire other possessions, some of which may be fairly necessary but certainly not of the same relative importance as a decent house over one's head.
What I have said is the personal side of the problem. How many times must these conditions be multiplied to encompass the housing shortage which fails to move the government to action? The pictures I have given may not be representative of all the housing shortage in Canada. They are true of parts of Toronto and I know they are true of parts of the capital city of thus country. They are probably general.
I wish to point out another aspect of this problem. Yesterday I called at a house. A veteran answered the door. He and his wife live there; the wife is expecting a child shortly. They have one room and the joint use of a kitchen. They pay $30 a month for that. In these days that sum is enough to provide that veteran and family with a house, not just a room and the joint use of a kitchen. For the most part the people are able to pay for decent accommodation, but that accommodation is not available and very little is being done to provide it for them.	*
As I have mentioned, there was a pre-war housing shortage. There was unemployment and there was a shortage of houses. It became worse during the war. There was no planning for the existing shortage, and perhaps for good reasons, because we could not make munitions and houses at the same time. But how the government expects to take care of a growing country and of returned soldiers whose families in the meantime had doubled up with in-laws and others, I do not know. What did the government expect to do with

800.000	men and women returning from the armed services? How were they to be housed when there was an acute shortage already?
How great is the housing crisis? In the spring of 1944 the advisory committee on housing and community planning estimated a shortage of 600,000 family units. The government made no preparation for large-scale building. It offered insufficient inducements after the war to war workers who had come from the smaller centres to the larger ones to return to their original abode. As quoted last Friday by my colleague, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), Brigadier Storms, now general manager of Housing Enterprises Limited, said in a published statement on March 14 last, that there are 375,000 families in Canada who are involuntarily doubled' up because of the housing shortage. In addition to this, although there may be some duplication, the Curtis report of three years ago estimated 300,000 sub-standard dwellings in Canada, and I can point to many sub-standard dwellings in my own riding. The need is colossal; it is urgent. The housing crisis constitutes a national emergency of the first order.
Last year the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) estimated that 39,000 new dwelling units. were built and 5,000 reconverted. That is an estimate, and many consider that it is substantially in excess of the actual number of houses which were provided. But even if we take it at its face value it is not enough, for it will never solve the problem which faces this country.
The economic system can be made to break the back of this housing shortage, but it will not be done by letting bad enough alone. An indignant people will not stand for it.
The government has never denied the responsibility for the housing crisis in Canada. No fewer than, three agencies of the government have helped to muddle the problem, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or its antecedent; Wartime Housing, and recently the Department of Veterans Affairs. Mr. H. C. Nichols, the retiring president of the Canadian Construction Association, stated on January 14 of this year that the capacity of the building industry in Canada to-day is
30.000	houses per annum, which is hardly enough to keep up with the current wear and tear without attacking the 375,000 backlog of needed houses.
What are the possibilities of solution at the government's present rate of progress? Obviously the people of Canada will not be decently housed in the near future.
In the face of this tremendous housing shortage there were 263,000 people reported

as unemployed at the end of February, 1946. It seems almost incredible that we should at one and the same time have a housing shortage of such dimensions and 263,000 people on the unemployed rolls. I should like to ask the minister how many men are being trained for the construction industry in the Department of Labour's training schools? The Minister of Reconstruction said he was alarmed at the rate of expansion of industry in Canada. May I ask, is all industry expanding and what industry is entitled to a higher priority than housing, and what expansion have we to show in that field? The Minister of Reconstruction says he is alarmed at the rate of expansion, and yet we find that housing is apparently relegated to a secondary position.
All mercantile housing, with only the most pressing exceptions, and theatre construction should be eliminated until the housing crisis is over. The house might be interested in knowing that the dwelling which I described in some detail with fifty-three people in it is to be torn down presently if a building permit is issued by the city, which it has not issued so far, and in its place is to be erected a motion-picture theatre. Certainly in this day wre must have some idea of what comes first, and surely housing comes ahead of more amusement centres.
The figures given by the Minister of Reconstruction''on the export of lumber only indicate that in the face of the need for domestic building more lumber should be retained at home. We are on a new domestic standard as compared with the pre-war years. In my riding one-third of the people badly need more of the necessities of life; another third need more of 'the good tilings of life, and the remaining third would not refuse a higher standard of living. With a national income now increased from three and a half billion to eight or nine billion dollars, 'and the price level not excessively out of line with what it was before the war, the whole question of production for export and domestic consumption should be examined. We are trying to export to the whole world not only as a measure of temporary and urgent relief, but in order to build up future trade. If we do not retain some of our exports we may find that our people will have to do without housing permanently. Instead of exporting unemployment, we are importing shortages and doing our level best to make our own people have a lower standard of living.
Take, for example, the figures for the newsprint industry, which means that more and more men are being used to cut pulp wood who could be cutting lumber, and these figures have been showing a steady expansion. Surely
Canadian newsprint, which is an industry with which I am familiar and in which I am interested, was not severely dealt with during the war in comparison with that of other countries, and yet we find to-day that it is able to expand its exports and use men to cut-down wood for pulp; whereas these same men could be used for producing more lumber in this country. Where is the control? Where is the direction which this government should exercise to meet the essential needs of our people?
What else should the government do to solve this crisis? ' I suggest and urge that they should adjust wage ceilings. Building materials were not considered a war necessity, and the wages of workers in those industries were held at virtually peace-time levels. If you look at the figures for bricklayers, for instance, you will find that they were held pretty much at their peace-time level. The result was that men in that industry left for war-time occupations, where wage rates were higher. Now that war industry is over, there is little inclination on their part to go back to the building industry, even at wage rates which are slightly higher than those in effect when they left that industry, and which are substantially below those which obtained in war industry.
Wartime Housing priorities disrupted the building industry. Small builders and private owners found that they could not get the materials they required because of the priorities which the government, under Wartime Housing placed upon the lumber and building supplies industries. There has been a shortage of building supplies not only because of the wage ceilings but because of the price ceilings. We must treat the national housing emergency as a crisis and allow a reasonable increase in wages so that more workers will be attracted into that field. More of those unemployed workers who to-day are looking for work must be taught how to engage in the building trades in order to render an essential and worthwhile service to their fellow Canadians. That was the practice we followed in connection with war industry. Peace-time occupations were frozen;, wages could not be increased. But when it came to aeroplane factories, munitions factories and so on, wage levels were advanced. Workers flowed into those higher paid jobs, naturally, and we did a thoroughly commendable job when it came to munitions. Now we must use the same tactics, the same principles if we are to solve this housing crisis which is upon our doorstep at the present time.
Let me offer another suggestion into which I believe the government should look. During the war not only had we to pay higher wages

to attract workers to war industries; we also found it necessary to build more war plants, and we allowed private builders the privilege of writing off the cost of those war additions over a short period of years, on the basis that after the war they would not be useful for the particular purpose for which they were built. Now I recommend that the government allow manufacturers of building supplies to create additions to their factories to meet this emergency, which may last for five years. It may last longer than that, but I do not' see how it can last for less. Then the government should allow' the owners of these industries to write off that excess capacity during the period of the crisis.
As an emergency measure I should like to recommend that the government grant first mortgage building loans at a rate as low at two per cent if necessary. If wages in the building industries are increased in order to get more workers, and if the cost of building supplies rise, we do not want our people and particularly our veterans to have to buy houses at inflated values. One of the greatest factors in the cost of a house is the cost of money. To-day the government is borrowing at 2% per cent per annum, and to meet this crisis it could well afford to lend money on first mortgage loans on new houses at a rate as low as two per cent. That would go a long way toward absorbing any additional cost brought about by the emergency measures I have suggested. Possibly the government should even consider subsidizing new construction. Buildings and houses are being subsidized in Great Britain in order to meet the acute shortage there, and our people, particularly in the low-income brackets, must be allowed to have decent shelter over their heads. If because of the wage rates in this country it should become necessary to subsidize building, then the government should do so.
Then I believe the government should withdraw from the field of actual construction and cease its interference with private builders. If the government wishes to maintain supervision, then let private industry do the building and, if necessary, purchase the complete housing units from the builders, who understand the business and can get things done.
There is not time to go into the matter of local taxation, which has made housing unprofitable for both individual owners and landlords. I shall say only this, that Wartime Housing has not proved as efficient, from the many examples which have come to our notice, as construction by private builders. The wartime prices and trade board is also one of the evils at the root of this jam we

are facing to-day. That board cannot know everyone's business and how businesses are interdependent. There are shortages of 'furnaces, because furnaces may not be sold at high enough prices. Therefore houses cannot be completed. Or it may be a shortage of soil pipe, or of porcelain insulators, which are examples that have been brought to my notice. Wartime Housing certainly is not in as good a position to get skilled help as are private contractors, many of whom have had the same men working with them for long periods of years. Instead of wrecking industry, the government should learn how to utilize it.
Building tradesmen should be given an incentive to work holidays and overtime; but if they are to have from thirty to fifty per cent of their extra wages taken in taxation they will not work more than the straight forty-hour week. I well recall the memorable words of a C.C.F. member in regard to his constituent, who was a mixed farmer and who found that he was being taxed on the extra cream he was able to obtain by working before breakfast in the morning and milking the cows after dinner at night, and who said, "I'll not milk cows for Ilsley." So he got rid of his herd. Human nature being what it is, I say it is folly to make laws which fly in the face of increased production. There is plenty of capital for investment in buildings; and with more take-home pay not only can workers produce more, but more workers will join the building trades.
The Liberal government has .become a big, cumbersome nuisance. It is preventing Canadians from using their natural ability to look after their - own needs. The war with Germany has now been over for nearly ten months and the Japanese war for nearly seven months, but the controllers still want to control. If the government will only give the horse its head we can rely on Canadian workers and Canadian industry to supply our housing requirements. If there is one thing we owe our returning veterans it is decent homes for themselves and their families. That is the prime duty of any government. The people expect some government planning and some direction as long as controls remain in force. Let the government make.it possible for our people, our economic system and our democracy to deliver the goods.
